goal: Third discovery wave: six domain agents on the six largest per-domain shortfalls (kitchen, lighting, security, automotive, computing, wearables), at 7 records each.
outcome: Partial. All six agents were terminated by the same session limit that killed wave 2, roughly 25 minutes in. Only the computing agent had finished writing; it produced all seven of its records. The other five died during research with nothing on disk.
findings: Peripherals were the right call. Five of the seven are D0 records in subcategories that had nothing at all — KVM, webcam, mouse, docking station, keyboard, switch — and they are the kind of record the catalog was missing: not arguments about whether a device can be liberated, just hardware that was never connected in the first place.

The two agents that reported before dying had both just confirmed FCC sibling-control cleanly (TP-Link, IOGEAR, and separately Schlage B60 documentation for security). The heuristic is holding up as the workhorse of D0 claims.

system_gaps_found.gap: qnap-ts-233-us was filed D2 with account_required 'for_setup', which is a REJECT trigger — the field contradicted the tier it was filed under. The cause was a genuine ambiguity, not carelessness: QTS setup does make you create an administrator account, but it is a credential stored on the NAS, not a QNAP account. The record's own rationale said as much while the field said otherwise.
system_gaps_found.fix: Corrected to 'none'. Added a PRINCIPLES rule distinguishing a local credential from a vendor account, with the test 'if the vendor went out of business tonight, could you still get in tomorrow?', and a validator rule failing any D0/D1/D2 record that claims a mandatory vendor account. D3 is exempt, since D3 means core function does need the cloud and a local path exists anyway. Audited the catalog: qnap was the only false positive, and sonoff-basicr2's for_core at D3 is correct.

system_gaps_found.gap: All seven records arrived with vendor_risk null. The agents had searched the ledger, found no entry, and declined to write a number — but 'no documented incident' is what 0 means on the scale, and null left them inconsistent with every other verified record in the catalog.
system_gaps_found.fix: Normalised to 0 across all verified records. The agents' caveat that no dedicated vendor audit was performed stays where it belongs, in open_questions.

honest_limitations: plugable-ud-3900 rests on a single manufacturer page. It clears the bar (one Class A) but it is the thinnest record in the batch and the agent flagged it as such.

The five dead agents produced nothing recoverable. Unlike wave 2, where partial output was salvageable from disk, this wave lost its research entirely — the agents were still gathering when they were killed.
Two waves in a row have now been killed by the same limit. The waves are sized for a budget that is not there. Wave 4 should run fewer agents, not more.
surprises: The most useful record of the wave was the one that was wrong. The QNAP account-field error is a false positive the catalog would generate over and over — every NAS, every router, every network camera makes you set an admin password at setup — and it would have rejected most of the good hardware in two domains. It surfaced only because a tier and a field disagreed, which is a thing a validator can check and a human reading the page never would.
